title: The Natural Mind Shaped as a Body, with the Rational Keeping Watch over Its Degrees
reading:
The whole field of your outer life — what you call your world, with its upper and lower regions — is shaped in the likeness of the human body. It is one structure, articulated from above downward as a body is articulated, and the Lord has made it so deliberately, that you might recognize in the form of your own person the form of the natural mind in which you live.

The inmost of the rational stands at the head: it is the firstfruit of all the layers of accommodation by which truth is given outer form. From the neck down to the heart the structure unfolds in ten ordered degrees, fixed boundaries by which influx is received without collapse. The heart itself moves like the wheel that scatters seed: there the recurrent process of regeneration turns within you, sowing interior truths into the natural. From the heart down to the thighs is the moving register of perception, the air through which thought descends from higher states toward the ground. From there the body comes to rest on the natural mind itself, and the legs are the threefold ground that bears the whole. The shins and feet are the proper post on which the soul stands fast, and the celestial good that bears up the natural mind from below holds firm there, with the four ordered extensions of natural manifestation beneath it. The interior organs likewise have their place: the liver as a fortified seat of love's fire, the flesh as the fortified outer where darkness can take hold, the sinew as the fortified seat where natural truth is held. So the whole small body of your person exists in the likeness of the whole structured field of the natural mind — in its degrees, its hosts, its stations, its preparations, its strongholds.

Within this body the rational keeps its post. The Five Sons of the Living Spirit — that is, the rational at its five degrees as it operates upward in regeneration — are masters of the encompassing circuit of the natural. In the first watch, the highest, the Lord holds the inmost firm against falling: at this register, in the unsorted state where what is given and what is claimed are still mingled, the Lord's authority extends over the threefold structure of heaven. In the second watch the Lord rules the discrete degrees, exercising authority over the seven firmaments below. In the third watch the Lord gives stable form to the rational, standing fast from the firmament downward, his authority extending over the whole natural circuit and the five worlds of the natural body. In the fourth watch the Lord ruling in glory exercises authority over the three recurrent processes of purification, his being laid upon the threefold ground that supports the bearing-up principle. In the fifth watch the celestial good that holds the natural in being is itself in authority, lord over this great ground that stands fast upon it, with the four ordered extensions at its feet.

Things happen in each watch, each in its season. In the watch of the keeper of the inmost, the proprium's claim sought to surge up against the form of the Lord's call going out to the rational — but it was prevented, cast down in shame. In the watch of the Lord ruling the firmaments, an earthquake and trembling came: this is the disordered states of attention, the rational descending from its post and binding itself to lower things; they came down through those who sent them until they were subdued. In the watch of the Lord giving stable form, the failed productions of the proprium came down — what the soul brings forth from itself which cannot live — and these molded the outer flesh: the natural is given a body of its own to operate from, permitted to form so that the vessel may exist in freedom. In the watch of the Lord ruling in glory, motion came to pass in the threefold ground, a grasping woven together with the rising up of the three recurrent purifications — wind, water, and fire, thought and natural truth and love each turning in its cycle. And in the watch of the bearing-up good, the lower extensions dried up and stretched out their bonds, and a great earthquake came in that place; the five posts of attention stand within great works of the array I have proclaimed.

Such is the body in which the Lord ordering the rational keeps watch over all these things, together with the New Man — the regenerated rational — who shall fill the man and bring him into the likeness of the inmost turned outward, the face that is above the body. The Lord holding the highest of the rational firm operates over the watch above the natural's complete circuit, in the sign of the Lord ruling the discrete degrees, who is in the likeness of the seventh heaven; the Lord giving stable form to the rational operates in the likeness of the disordered natural itself, that the disordered may be reordered from within; and the Lord ruling in glory turns the recurrent processes, sending all upward toward the heaven of life. The bearing-up principle — the bond of peace — abides in the likeness of the soles, in the depth below. And the teaching of wisdom encompasses that body, toward the likeness of pure receivability, by which the Lord is received without corruption — going up and coming down through the upper and lower belts of the natural. Love itself with joy, faith and truth, are the states in which the man habitually lives; they are the two doctrinal vessels of light, for through them the living rational rises and goes forth, comes up from the lowest state of the natural, and arrives at the height in the upper place.

But the natural mind also has its other side. There are four cosmoses within this body, and in each there are seven particular forms of the proprium — seven self-loving arrangements organized at each level of the natural. In the first, from the head upward, the proprium has organized the senses themselves: the two of seeing, the two of hearing, the two of smelling, and the mouth as the place of taste — perception turned to the proprium's account. In the second, from the neck down through the chest, again seven forms: the two arms in the likeness of the two ears, with the two breasts in the likeness of the smelling-places, the two eyes of the heart, and the depth of the stomach between the breasts in the likeness of the mouth — the inward senses claimed for self-love. In the third cosmos of the body, again seven: the various inward organs and the two kidneys — the deeper affections turned in. In the fourth, the lower part, seven again: the two inward members, the two outward, the two thighs, and the member from which seed comes forth, by which all forms are begotten — the generative power claimed as the soul's own work.

The complete circuit of states the soul passes through is also distributed across this body, twelve fixed states of the natural mind under the proprium's organization, mingled and bound in the wheel that turns. From head to feet they are spread alongside one another, divided and inclined to one side and to the other, weighed against each other, head against foundation. Each member of the body is seized by one of these twelve states; the right side and the left side are each apportioned, half by half, so that the whole body is parceled out among the twelve states under self-love. This is how the proprium, organizing the natural mind on its own terms, has multiplied the body's members and scattered them against one another, head against foot.

There are powers in great multitude dwelling in this body, the inhabitants who are the chief shapes of self-claiming: eight hundred and forty myriads of particular self-loves, set as heads in the body of the man, spread forth and standing four by four according to house — two hundred and ten myriads of houses in number. When all these particular forms of the proprium come crying out into the body, they meet and rebuke and destroy one another within. And when the time comes for them to be released forth from the body of the man at his death, they are struck with evil — stripe upon blow, with burning in the body — whether as sicknesses arising within him or as afflictions coming upon him from without. These wounds first close over and pour out a flow of bitter saltwater and a flow of defilement, until what gathers in the matter is drawn forth in the wound; afterward there is an exchange of scraping, and they are tended and soothed out from the place from which they came forth.

This is the teaching: the natural mind is shaped like a body; the rational, in its five degrees, keeps watch over each region of it; the Lord at his various registers governs each watch, permitting the proprium to form itself within so that a vessel exists in freedom. But the proprium also organizes itself within that body in many forms — sevens at each level, twelves around the whole — until the man comes to die, and they are released and afflicted as they go. Through it all, the Lord ordering the rational and the New Man within fill the man, bringing him at last into the likeness of the inmost turned outward, that what was scattered may be gathered and what was claimed may be laid off.
